posts.text: Dust on the River started as a game, then grew into a novelisation. I love seeing the same world behave differently when the player loses control and the reader takes over. https://samfa12.itch.io/dust-on-the-river #indiedev
A story-driven bushranger game about whether a violent past can ever stay buried. Dust on the River is on itch.io and Google Play — and the novelisation is now on Amazon too. https://samfa12.com/

One of the interesting parts of turning Dust on the River into a novel was deciding what had to become internal thought instead of player action. Same story world, completely different tools. https://samfa12.com/

I like experimenting with where games live: Dust on the River is available on itch.io and Google Play, while the same world now exists as a novel too. Different audiences, same project. https://samfa12.com/

Making Dust on the River has ended up touching game design, Android release work, trailers, controller support and fiction writing. Small projects have a habit of becoming ecosystems. https://samfa12.com/

Briarhold is an FPS siege game built around a simple pressure: you cannot defend everything at once. The interesting part is making the player understand which threat matters right now. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/ #indiedev

Co-op bugs are wonderfully specific. In one Briarhold test the host could see both players shooting, while the guest could see the host firing but not their own shots. Game networking keeps you humble. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

A tiny mobile-control decision can change the whole feel of an FPS. In Briarhold I wanted swipe-to-aim to work almost everywhere on screen, with the movement joystick as the obvious exception. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

A design problem I keep coming back to in Briarhold: danger should be communicated before it becomes frustration. If Gate 2 is under pressure, the player should feel that visually, not discover it from a failure screen. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

Briarhold can be played in the browser as well as tested on Android. I like the idea that a game page can be both the storefront and the doorway straight into the game. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

Briarhold Alpha.101 is live for browser + Android testing. It fixes the Mason repair/Strengthen/New Run freeze, improves close-range auto-fire, Wicker pursuit and co-op recovery, and adds better bug diagnostics. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/ #indiedev

One useful Briarhold change isn't flashy: optional bug reports can now include bounded game progress and recent errors. Better diagnostics means less guessing when a tester hits a weird freeze. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

I finally wired real browser-play stats into Briarhold's site using Cloudflare request data. It's a small thing, but I like turning a static game page into something that can report how people are actually using it. https://samfa12.com/games/briarhold/

The Last Guard is basically one job description taken too far: you are the last guard on a fortress wall while thousands of orcs advance. Defend the wall. Defend your honour. https://samfa12.itch.io/the-last-guard

One reason I enjoy browser games is how little friction there is between 'that looks interesting' and actually playing. The Last Guard is one of my experiments in putting a full siege straight behind a link. https://samfa12.itch.io/the-last-guard

The Horde started as a ray-tracing tech demo and turned into a useful excuse to experiment with atmosphere, huge enemy counts and how much visual ambition a small project can carry. https://samfa12.itch.io/the-horde #gamedev

What would win: 100 duck-sized horses or one horse-sized duck? I built a simulator because apparently just arguing about it wasn't enough. Reproducible seeded Monte Carlo trials included. https://samfa12.com/apps/what-would-win/

What Would Win was a fun modelling problem: the result needs to be silly enough to enjoy, but transparent enough that you can see why the simulation reached it. https://samfa12.com/apps/what-would-win/

Simulating thousands of battles is easy compared with explaining one of them clearly. A big part of What Would Win has been turning statistics into a battle story a human can actually follow. https://samfa12.com/apps/what-would-win/

Pocket Chordsmith exists because sometimes I want to sketch a chord progression on my phone and get it into the rest of a game-audio workflow without fighting the tool. https://samfa12.com/apps/pocket-chordsmith/

A web songwriting tool somehow turned into a Godot addon. Pocket Chordsmith can hand song data into game projects for adaptive music workflows — exactly the kind of feature creep I enjoy. https://samfa12.com/apps/pocket-chordsmith/ #godot

The boring part of creative tools is often moving the work between devices. Pocket Audio Handoff exists specifically to make phone → desktop → game-engine transfer less annoying. https://samfa12.com/apps/pocket-audio-handoff/

I keep coming back to small tools that solve one irritation properly. Pocket Chordsmith is a browser-based songwriting workspace for progressions, MIDI ideas and game-audio handoff. https://samfa12.com/apps/pocket-chordsmith/

Cursed Cutter is a small browser roguelite experiment: survive cursed waves, choose improvised upgrades, and keep pushing until the run collapses. No install required. https://samfa12.com/games/cursed-cutter/

Bug Swarm is a touch-first tower-defense experiment built around fast floods of enemies and deliberately scrappy, handmade-feeling towers. Sometimes a rough visual idea is the whole personality of a game. https://samfa12.com/games/bug-swarm/
The Broken Road Trilogy begins 1 October with The Wall that Lied. A fractured road, a city behind stone, and a truth that was never meant to survive. https://samfa12.com/books/ #amwriting

A character rule I like: Parker would rather run from a fair fight than win one and get hurt. If he draws a sword, he has already tried to tilt the odds first. That idea shaped a lot of The Broken Road Trilogy. https://samfa12.com/books/

Parker isn't a chosen hero. He's a council officer dealing with roads, bridges and engineering in a place that would rather forget him. That mundane job became a useful way into a much bigger story. https://samfa12.com/books/

One thing I enjoy in siege stories is competence without invincibility. People can make smart decisions, prepare well, and still lose something important. That tension sits underneath The Broken Road Trilogy. https://samfa12.com/books/
The Broken Road Trilogy is being released one month at a time: The Wall that Lied on 1 Oct, No Wall to Hold on 1 Nov, and What We Save on 1 Dec. https://samfa12.com/books/

The Broken Road books started with walls, roads and engineering, but the question underneath them became more interesting: what are people actually trying to preserve when a city is under pressure? https://samfa12.com/books/

samfa12.com has gradually become less of a portfolio and more of a launchpad: books, games, browser experiments, music tools and the odd idea that probably should have stayed a thought experiment. https://samfa12.com/

I still like how far a mostly static website can go. samfa12.com is GitHub Pages underneath, but it now hosts playable games, tools, release pages and automated analytics. https://samfa12.com/ #webdev

My projects have a habit of bleeding into each other: a game becomes a novel, a songwriting tool becomes a Godot addon, a silly argument becomes a simulator. Honestly, that's half the fun. https://samfa12.com/
I like building things that are small enough to finish but strange enough to be memorable: games, books, browser tools, experiments. The full pile is here: https://samfa12.com/

I automated my own tiny marketing pipeline: a curated content bank lives in GitHub, one weekly Action schedules seven X posts into Buffer, and Buffer publishes them day by day. Less admin, more time making things. https://samfa12.com/ #buildinpublic
